↳   How we estimated thisThe data, the defaults & the unknowns ＋

A transparent estimate, not a promise

Route: Managed aerobic composting → finished compost → soil. Process version: evidence-v1.

No validated material-specific process retention model included. Application fraction 100% is a scenario boundary, not an observed recovery rate.

Each amount = fresh component mass × fresh-weight concentration × its element-specific retention × fraction applied. Dry-weight values are converted using dry-matter fraction first. Retention already accounts for losses; no extra compost-yield multiplier is applied.

portion-v1: banana flesh 118g (USDA medium); orange flesh 131g (USDA common portion). Banana peel 60g, orange peel 45g, apple flesh 154g / peel 26g / core 20g are assumed household defaults. No weighing required; editable.

Composition versus returned nutrients

Seed composition is per 100 g raw fresh material, checked against USDA SR28 (2015). The FoodData Central cross-reference identifies the corresponding SR Legacy entry. A source average is not a measurement of your scrap.

Calcium, magnesium, sulfur and trace-element returns remain unknown without validated retention factors. Sodium is not counted as a soil benefit.

What these cards don’t measure

Carbon returned is carbon applied in finished compost: it is different from carbon originally in food, carbon remaining years later, or net greenhouse-gas emissions avoided. It is not permanent sequestration.

Food moisture, compost moisture at application, soil water management and water used to grow food are separate. Much food moisture evaporates. We do not estimate litres saved or water returned; composting does not recover growing water.

Leaves or wood may be needed. Their mass, carbon and nutrients are excluded from the food contribution.

Missing values stay unknown, never zero. Feedipedia data is excluded pending reuse permission. No pomace or mixed citrus pulp substitutes are used.

03 / THE BIGGER PICTURE

More than nutrients.
A foundation for life.

When appropriately composted and returned to soil, organic material can support the systems that keep soil healthy.

Explore the science at EPA ↗
01

A living community

Supports soil organisms and the cycling of nutrients.

02

Room to put down roots

Helps build stable soil structure for root growth.

03

Water that finds its way

Supports water infiltration and retention.

04

Soil that stays in place

Helps soil resist erosion.

Every soil has a different starting point. Not every soil needs more nutrients, and compost alone cannot reverse every kind of degradation. Test soil and follow local composting guidance.
